Helicoverpa zea: One caterpillar, several crop names: corn earworm, tomato fruitworm, cotton bollworm. Its host-hopping makes crop context part of the ID story.
Helicoverpa armigera: This caterpillar has a menu of 100+ host plants. A pest with that many options can connect very different cropping systems.
Spodoptera frugiperda: Fall armyworm larvae can eat one another when crowded in a corn whorl. Even a pest outbreak has a food-web story.
Spodoptera exigua: The beet armyworm is no beet specialist: it feeds on many vegetable and field crops, so the crop name alone won't tell you where it can turn up.
Spodoptera eridania: Young southern armyworms feed in groups, then spread out as they grow. The same pest can change its footprint within a crop.
Ostrinia nubilalis: The European corn borer likely reached the US around 1910 hidden in imported broomcorn.
Agrotis ipsilon: Black cutworm moths can ride spring storm winds north from the Gulf states into the Corn Belt.
Plutella xylostella: Diamondback moth has evolved resistance to many insecticides: a vivid reminder that pest control is an evolutionary arms race, not a one-and-done fix.
Trichoplusia ni: Cabbage looper cells in the lab can manufacture proteins. A crop pest can also become a useful tool for biotechnology.
Pieris rapae: The small white butterfly reached Quebec in the 1860s and now follows cabbage across North America.
Chrysodeixis includens: Soybean loopers walk by looping: they arch their backs like tiny green inchworms.
Anticarsia gemmatalis: A disturbed velvetbean caterpillar may thrash about and drop off the plant.
Manduca sexta: Hornworm moths hover at flowers like hummingbirds, and the caterpillar is a lab model for insect biology.
Pectinophora gossypiella: Pink bollworm larvae feed hidden inside cotton bolls, out of easy sight. The US declared it eradicated from cotton in 2018 after a major area-wide campaign.
Cydia pomonella: That 'worm in the apple' is often a codling moth caterpillar.
Aspila molesta: Orchards can be filled with synthetic female scent so male moths get confused and cannot find mates.
Phthorimaea absoluta: The tomato leafminer was reported in Spain in 2006 and has since traveled across Africa and Asia.
Diatraea saccharalis: In Brazil, tiny parasitoid wasps are released against sugarcane borer. Pest management can recruit a natural enemy instead of relying on one control tactic.
Chilo suppressalis: Rice stem borer damage has a dramatic name: 'deadheart', when the central shoot of a young rice plant dies.
Leptinotarsa decemlineata: The Colorado potato beetle switched from a wild nightshade to potatoes in the 1800s, then went on a world tour.
Diabrotica virgifera: Some western corn rootworm populations lay eggs in soybean fields, dodging the classic corn-soybean rotation. Pest behavior can reshape a management plan.
Diabrotica undecimpunctata: Its Latin name says 'eleven-spotted', but the adult actually has twelve spots.
Anthonomus grandis: A boll weevil monument in Enterprise, Alabama thanks the pest for pushing local farming to diversify. Sometimes a pest changes the whole agricultural story.
Cerotoma trifurcata: Bean leaf beetles come in several colors and spot patterns, which makes ID a good challenge.
Epilachna varivestis: This bean-eating beetle is a lady beetle relative, but unlike many lady beetles it feeds on plants. Family resemblance is no guarantee of ecological role.
Phyllotreta striolata: Flea beetles jump like fleas thanks to enlarged hind legs.
Psylliodes chrysocephala: Despite the 'flea' in its name it is a beetle, and it jumps with big hind legs.
Brassicogethes aeneus: Pollen beetles love yellow: an oilseed rape field can host thousands.
Sitona lineatus: Pea leaf weevils leave scalloped notches on leaf edges, like someone with tiny scissors.
Oulema melanopus: Cereal leaf beetle larvae wear a coat of their own droppings. The crop-damaging stage can be surprisingly hard to spot.
Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus: Rice water weevil larvae live in flooded paddies, getting air from rice roots.
Popillia japonica: Japanese beetles were first found in the US in 1916, in a New Jersey nursery.
Conotrachelus nenuphar: Plum curculio females cut a little crescent-shaped scar in fruit to lay an egg.
Agriotes lineatus: Wireworms become click beetles, which flip themselves into the air with a click when upside down.
Sitophilus oryzae: A rice weevil lays an egg inside a grain and plugs the tiny hole. The next generation develops where a quick surface check can't see it.
Tribolium castaneum: The red flour beetle was the first beetle to have its genome sequenced (2008).
Aphis glycines: After its North American discovery in 2000, soybean aphid spread across the soybean belt within years. Early detection matters when a tiny sap-feeder multiplies fast.
Aphis gossypii: Cotton aphids range from pale yellow to nearly black depending on conditions.
Myzus persicae: Green peach aphids can transmit more than 100 plant viruses. Their crop impact can travel in a mouthpart-sized package.
Rhopalosiphum padi: Bird cherry-oat aphids have two homes: bird cherry trees in winter, cereals in summer.
Rhopalosiphum maidis: Aphid daughters can already carry embryos of the next generation. Under good conditions, population growth can become a generational relay.
Sitobion avenae: Ants sometimes guard aphids for their sugary honeydew. A crop pest can be part of a surprisingly cooperative food-web partnership.
Acyrthosiphon pisum: Pea aphids can be red or green, and some pigment genes have fungal origins. Even a familiar field pest has an unexpected evolutionary backstory.
Bemisia tabaci: The name Bemisia tabaci covers a complex of look-alike whiteflies. Getting the identity right is the first step before comparing biology or risk.
Trialeurodes vaporariorum: Tap a greenhouse tomato and clouds of greenhouse whiteflies may rise. A disturbance can reveal what a still leaf was hiding.
Diaphorina citri: Adult Asian citrus psyllids feed with their rear ends tilted up in the air.
Nilaparvata lugens: A brown planthopper outbreak can leave rice patches looking scorched, a symptom farmers call hopperburn. The damage pattern tells a field story.
Empoasca fabae: Potato leafhoppers walk sideways, like tiny crabs.
Lygus lineolaris: The tarnished plant bug is named for its mottled look, like an old silver spoon.
Lygus hesperus: Lygus feeding can leave strawberries lumpy and misshapen, a symptom called cat-facing. Tiny feeding marks can have a very visible crop outcome.
Halyomorpha halys: In autumn, brown marmorated stink bugs gather on house walls looking for a warm place to overwinter.
Nezara viridula: The southern green stink bug can turn brownish in cooler months.
Euschistus servus: Stink bugs 'stink' because of defensive chemicals released from scent glands.
Megacopta cribraria: The kudzu bug was first found in Georgia in 2009 and spread across the Southeast within a few years.
Murgantia histrionica: The harlequin bug wears a flashy orange-and-black costume.
Anasa tristis: Squash bug eggs sit in neat bronze clusters on the undersides of leaves.
Leptoglossus phyllopus: 'Leaf-footed' refers to the flattened, leaf-like expansions on the hind legs.
Lycorma delicatula: Spotted lanternfly is neither a fly nor a lantern: it's a planthopper. Common names can mislead, so field monitoring starts with a reliable ID.
Frankliniella occidentalis: 'Thrips' is both singular and plural: one thrips, two thrips.
Thrips tabaci: Onion thrips are only 1-2 mm long, but their silvery feeding scars are easy to spot.
Tetranychus urticae: Two-spotted spider mites are arachnids, not insects, and can web a leaf like a miniature tent. The pest you miss at first can leave a very visible trace.
Drosophila suzukii: Unlike many fruit flies associated with overripe fruit, spotted-wing drosophila can lay eggs in ripening fruit. That timing changes the crop-protection challenge.
Ceratitis capitata: Medfly programs have released sterile males by the millions. Here, control works by interrupting reproduction rather than spraying the adult population.
Bactrocera dorsalis: Male oriental fruit flies are strongly attracted to methyl eugenol, a plant compound used in monitoring traps. A scent can turn an invisible population into a count.
Delia radicum: Gardeners put little collars around cabbage seedlings to stop this fly laying eggs.
Melanoplus differentialis: The differential grasshopper has black herringbone marks on its hind legs.
Locusta migratoria: Crowding can change locust color, shape and behavior: solitary grasshoppers can become swarmers. Population density itself can change the risk picture.
Schistocerca gregaria: A desert locust can eat roughly its own weight in plants each day.
Solenopsis invicta: Fire ants survive floods by linking together into living rafts.
Hippodamia convergens: This lady beetle's name points to two white lines that meet on its thorax. A quick field mark can help distinguish a helpful predator from a crop pest.
Harmonia axyridis: When threatened, Asian lady beetles 'reflex bleed' a smelly yellow fluid from their leg joints.
Coccinella septempunctata: Seven spots make this lady beetle easy to recognize, but its larvae are predators too. Beneficial insects don't stay in their adult form forever.
Adalia bipunctata: The two-spot ladybird comes as red with black spots or black with red spots, same species.
Coleomegilla maculata: This lady beetle eats pollen as well as aphids and insect eggs. A flexible diet can keep a beneficial predator in the field between pest meals.
Chrysoperla carnea: Green lacewing larvae are called aphid lions; adults also use pollen and nectar. The same beneficial species can have very different diets at different life stages.
Chrysoperla rufilabris: Lacewing eggs sit on tiny silk stalks, away from hungry siblings.
Orius insidiosus: Minute pirate bugs hunt thrips, mites and insect eggs. A predator's broad menu can make it a useful ally—and a species worth recognizing in crop assessments.
Geocoris punctipes: Big-eyed bugs hunt eggs and small insects. Look closely before calling every insect on a crop a pest.
Nabis roseipennis: Damsel bugs ambush prey with grasping front legs, despite the delicate name.
Podisus maculiventris: The spined soldier bug is a predatory stink bug that attacks caterpillars. A familiar pest-shaped silhouette can belong to a beneficial species.
Perillus bioculatus: This predatory stink bug feeds on Colorado potato beetle larvae. In a crop, the identity of the stink bug matters.
Zelus longipes: Assassin bugs inject saliva that liquefies prey from the inside.
Calosoma scrutator: Its common name is 'fiery searcher': a glittering caterpillar-hunting ground beetle.
Pterostichus melanarius: This ground beetle works the night shift, eating slugs, weed seeds and insects.
Poecilus cupreus: 'Cupreus' means coppery, and it gleams like a new penny.
Harpalus pensylvanicus: Its species name spells Pennsylvania with one 'n', an older spelling.
Aleochara bilineata: Aleochara larvae hunt cabbage root fly pupae and develop inside the fly's puparium. A natural enemy can target a pest while it is hidden underground.
Cotesia congregata: Hornworms covered in white cocoons look sprinkled with rice; those are wasp cocoons.
Aphidius ervi: A parasitized aphid becomes a golden mummy, then the tiny wasp cuts a round exit hole. Biological control can leave its own field evidence.
Trichopoda pennipes: Feather-legged flies glue eggs onto stink bugs, which then carry them around.
Toxomerus politus: Hover flies mimic wasps but cannot sting; their larvae can eat aphids. One insect can look like a threat as an adult and act as a crop ally as a larva.
Allograpta obliqua: Hover flies can hover in place and even fly backward. Their larvae can be aphid predators, while adults visit flowers.
Episyrphus balteatus: Marmalade hoverflies migrate across Europe in huge numbers. A beneficial insect can move across landscapes, not just between neighboring rows.
Forficula auricularia: Despite the ear myth, earwig mothers guard their eggs and tend their young.
Pardosa milvina: Wolf spider mothers carry their egg sacs, then their spiderlings on their backs.
Oxyopes salticus: Lynx spiders pounce on prey like tiny cats.
Phidippus audax: Jumping spiders have excellent vision for their size, and bold jumpers will stare right back.
Phytoseiulus persimilis: Predatory mites can arrive in a bottle and be released onto crops to hunt spider mites. Biological control can be small enough to pour.
Neoseiulus californicus: This predatory mite can switch to pollen when spider mites are scarce. That alternative food may help a natural enemy persist between pest outbreaks.
Apis mellifera: A worker honey bee's lifetime honey contribution is tiny—often estimated at about 1/12 teaspoon. Pollination, not an individual bee's honey, is the bigger field service.
Bombus impatiens: Bumble bees buzz-pollinate by vibrating flowers to shake pollen loose, which helps tomatoes set fruit. A flower visit can be a specialized tool, not just a stop for nectar.
Bombus terrestris: Bumble bees warm their flight muscles by shivering, letting them forage on cool days. Pollinator activity depends on more than whether flowers are present.
Bombus vosnesenskii: The yellow-faced bumble bee is a native western pollinator. Its field-margin and crop-foraging story is a reminder that exposure can extend beyond the planted field.
Bombus bimaculatus: Each spring, one bumble bee queen starts a colony from scratch. The timing of a pollinator's life cycle matters when thinking about seasonal exposure.
Osmia lignaria: Blue orchard bees nest in hollow tunnels and seal each brood cell with mud. Their offspring develop in a built environment, not in the open air.
Osmia bicornis: Red mason bees nest in hollow tubes and provision separate brood cells. A pollinator's nesting habitat can be part of its exposure story.
Osmia cornifrons: Hornfaced bees have been managed in Japanese apple orchards for decades. This small native bee can be a working part of an orchard's pollination system.
Megachile rotundata: Alfalfa leafcutting bees punch neat circles from leaves to line their nests. The crop pollinator also interacts directly with plant tissue.
Nomia melanderi: Alkali bees nest in dense underground 'bee cities'. A field's bare soil can be habitat, not empty space.
Xenoglossa pruinosa: Squash bees visit squash flowers at dawn, and males may sleep inside them. If you only look at midday, you can miss a pollinator's schedule.
Habropoda laboriosa: The blueberry bee is a specialist pollinator of blueberry flowers. Crop and wild pollinators don't all visit the same plants in the same way.
Agapostemon virescens: Some sweat bees visit flowers and are also attracted to salt in sweat. Pollinator behavior can be more varied than a simple flower-to-flower loop.
Melissodes bimaculatus: Male longhorn bees sleep while gripping plant stems with their jaws. A field after dark can still be pollinator habitat.
Eristalis tenax: The drone fly's aquatic larva breathes through a telescopic snorkel. A familiar flower visitor has a very different, water-dwelling early life stage.
Danaus plexippus: Monarch migration spans generations: no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. Protecting a migratory pollinator means thinking beyond one field and one season.
Daphnia magna: Water fleas are transparent enough to see a heartbeat under a microscope. In ecotoxicology, the test animal is small—but the response is visible.
Daphnia pulex: Daphnia pulex was among the first crustaceans to have its genome sequenced. This tiny freshwater animal has a big place in aquatic biology.
Chironomus riparius: Chironomid larvae are called bloodworms because hemoglobin turns them red. They live in sediment, making the bottom of a water body part of their story.
Gammarus fasciatus: This scud is an amphipod, a small crustacean—not a shrimp or an insect. Its place in freshwater food webs makes the group useful to know.
Chironomus dilutus: The familiar adult midge is brief; much of its life is spent as an aquatic larva. For sediment-dwelling species, the life stage can determine the exposure route.
Gammarus pulex: Freshwater shrimp shred fallen leaves into smaller pieces that feed stream food webs. A small crustacean helps move energy through the ecosystem.
Hexagenia limbata: Hexagenia mayfly hatches can be so immense they appear on weather radar. A pulse of insects can move aquatic production onto land in a single night.
Cloeon dipterum: Unlike most mayflies, this species can give birth to live young. Even familiar indicator groups can break the textbook pattern.
Pteronarcys californica: The salmonfly hatch is a feast for trout—and a seasonal event anglers plan around. Mayflies connect stream health to the food above the water, too.
Eisenia fetida: Tiger worms turn food scraps into compost. As soil recyclers, they make a memorable ambassador for why ecotoxicology looks below ground.
Lumbricus terrestris: Darwin's last book celebrated earthworms. Their burrowing reshapes soil, so a worm is more than a small animal in a test dish.
Folsomia candida: This tiny springtail is white, eyeless and reproduces without males. It is also a soil-dweller—an easy reminder that ecotoxicology isn't only about water.
Armadillidium vulgare: Pill bugs are land-living crustaceans, not insects. They feed among damp leaf litter, where soil and decomposing material meet.
Drosophila melanogaster: Fruit flies have flown in space and helped answer big biology questions. A familiar lab model can make complex effects easier to study.
Lumbriculus variegatus: Blackworms can regrow after injury. Their remarkable biology is a reminder that survival alone doesn't describe every effect on an organism.
Striacosta albicosta: Despite its name, corn is a main host of the western bean cutworm in much of the Corn Belt.
Melanaphis sacchari: Sugarcane aphids can reproduce without mating, so a few founders can become a fast-growing colony. Population growth is part of the crop-risk story.
Piezodorus guildinii: The reddish band across its back is the redbanded stink bug's giveaway.
Chloridea virescens: The tobacco budworm is also called the geranium budworm for its taste in flowers.
Novius cardinalis: The vedalia beetle helped control cottony cushion scale in citrus. It is a classic reminder that natural enemies can change the outcome of a pest problem.
Trissolcus japonicus: The samurai wasp is only millimeters long and attacks stink bug eggs. A beneficial insect can act before a crop pest ever hatches.
Melipona quadrifasciata: Stingless bees cannot sting, but some will crawl into your hair and bite.
Pimephales promelas: Male fathead minnows guard their eggs. Reproduction and parental behavior are part of fish biology—not just whether an adult survives.
Lemna minor: Duckweed mostly multiplies by cloning, even though it is a flowering plant. Its rapid growth makes changes in a tiny floating plant easy to notice.
Ceriodaphnia dubia: Water flea mothers can produce clonal young without mating. That can make lab populations more uniform, while reminding us that real populations also vary.
Varroa destructor: Varroa is named after the Roman author Varro, who wrote about bees.
Photinus pyralis: 'Femme fatale' fireflies (Photuris) mimic its flashes to lure and eat the males.
Brachinus fumans: Bombardier beetles fire a hot, pulsing chemical spray: a tiny jet engine.
